For clarification, can we ask the witness if the 100 soldiers belonging to the Serbian 14th Light Brigade observed by one corps are the same or are different from the 40 to 60 Serbian soldiers observed by the other corps? So what is the total number of people that we are looking for here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You've heard the question, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot confirm whether it goes for the same soldiers or some other soldiers, first of all, because it goes for reports originating from different units. Another thing I would like to point your attention to is an element which may be of importance, and that is that we are dealing with information that was still being verified. It says here they are still being verified. Another thing. It is stated here: "It is estimated by us," which is not a statement, it is part and parcel of our work. And another thing that must be borne in mind, and we saw it at one place, that everything was based on statements by prisoners of war, so first of all we have to establish when they were questioned, and this is part of the reports. And what they can tell us are just information that they provided, so we must take into account the value of the source of such information, and we must ask ourselves the question: What are the estimating powers of a common soldier or an officer which prevailed at the time when these statements were taken? And what we did with our reports, we drafted them a couple of days later, so we tried to understand the author's intentions in stating things in their report, and we must take into account the overall situation during combat activities, where a situation changes from minute to minute, from hour to hour. So this is a very intense situation, so it is impossible for me to answer, with any degree of certainty, your question or to confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you, for the benefit of the Chamber, just explain what the size of a reinforced infantry battalion, as mentioned in the document marked for identification 633? What is the strength of a reinforced infantry battalion, Mr. Husic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, a reinforced infantry battalion is usually reinforced by a company, and one company usually numbers 100 people. Of course, if we're dealing with an infantry company, an infantry battalion usually contains three to four companies, so we can take that it goes for 400 or 500 people, generally speaking, about a reinforced infantry battalion. So in this concrete example, this could be the number, but we have to take into account the operative word being it is our estimate. But when we referred to a wider area, we are discussing an area which has the capacity to house so many people, which does not have to be so at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have two documents left, and we'll try to complete them very quickly. The next document to be shown is PT2684.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Since the signature is already shown here, who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: This document is signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could go for a moment -- scroll to the right-hand side of the B/C/S, because here is some handwriting in the upper right-hand side. And in the translation, this handwriting is not reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you read out -- first of all, whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you read out what you wrote at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I sent the message to the author, Mr. Mrkaljevic, Sejfulah, and it can be seen from his initials. I state here "Mrki," which is his nickname, "this should be followed through with a view to realisation," and then I signed it, which means that he was supposed to follow up on this, meaning whether the unit that this document was sent to -- could you scroll to the left, please, a bit in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Please go to the left, please. The B/C/S version only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: And given that this is a document which requests for intelligence and is addressed to the Command of the 37th Division, meaning that this is our request sent to them to deliver intelligence, and my note to Mr. Mrkaljevic is to the effect of him checking whether the Command of the 37th Division fulfilled the demand or request that we -- is contained in this document. This would be my explanation for this handwritten note.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if you could just elucidate on the request here. It states in the document there is interest shown by representatives of the SA and MO. What does "SA" and "MO" stand for?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: "SA" and "MO" is acronyms for foreign armies and international organisations respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So there was an interest shown by representatives of foreign armies and international organisations. If I can quote here: "About the current lines of advance, on other fronts, possible intentions and expectations, the presence of Mujahedin and war crimes committed during the liberation of Vozuca." Could you explain a little bit what you were referring to here in your document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can provide you with an opinion about this. Your document -- "reference, your document, strictly confidential number ..." et cetera, et cetera, at the beginning of this document, this means that there exists another document sent by this division to us. And under item 2, which regulates the action of foreign armies and international organisations in the zone of responsibility of that division, there had been sent to them a note expressing their interest. And given that we are dealing with an extraordinary activity, we expected them to provide us with an explanation, why was this extraordinary. When referring to representatives of foreign armies and international organisations, all had their areas of responsibility and their liaison officers, and their representatives contacted our offices in those areas. In this specific case, bearing in mind what they requested, it is evident that their area of interest was broader than the area where they operated, and this seemed to us interesting, and this is why we requested that these be explained or expanded upon or clarified, so that we would be sure that there was no mistake there. It is stated here that they're interested in the area of Jajce, but officers coming to the 37th Division headquarters which was seated in Tesanj came from Doboj. Their interest could be suggested from some other side, but in any case, bearing in mind that in this case they showed interest for other areas as well, not only that but also the possible intentions, expectations, et cetera, this is reflected here. What is referred to are El Mujahedin and war crimes committed during the liberation of Vozuca. This is a tendention, because representatives of foreign armies and international organisations are not those who would establish that war crimes had been committed or not, and this was tendentious in our view, and that is why we sought explanation, because intelligence officers are obliged to relay requests without altering the contents of their requests. If they said "war crimes," we relayed "war crimes." So we sought clarification about these requests so that we can process them, and this would be my explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You're sending this here to the 37th Division. Did you make also internal inquiries, if any, about the document sent by the 37th Division, containing the issue of Mujahedin and war crimes?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "What do you mean internal," correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With "internal", I meant within the 3rd Corps itself. You're sending it to a division here; we can see from the address you list, it goes to the Command of the 37th Division. My question is: Did you also inquiry internally within the 3rd Corps itself about the validity of allegations about the presence of Mujahedin and war crimes committed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, was the 37th Division not part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It was, but I'm asking whether he inquired within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But asking from the 37th Division is asking from within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant -- I have to clarify myself. I meant within the 3rd Corps Staff, within the headquarter itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's much different. That's why the witness doesn't understand.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't believe so, for the simple reason because through this document, we are seeking from the 37th Division explanations, what they wrote under item 2 of their supposed report. If you are referring to the section of the document addressees, and it is stated here: "Delivered to 3rd Corps," to the acknowledgment of the 3rd Corps, without any obligations attached thereto, what needs to be established is what were the intentions of the author. But whoever needs to do some explanation is the author, and this is why we addressed this request for intelligence to them and not to anybody else. And another thing. Reference is being made to war crimes, but this is not the only thing in the document. There are other things; the relations between the ARBiH and HVO in the region of Jajce is far above the responsibilities of those units which were seated in Doboj. So it is indicative of a level of interest on the part of those representatives in the area of Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I ask that the document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will. Before we do so, I just want a few things to be clarified here with you, Mr. Husic. Did you have any knowledge of what war crimes are being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this part of -- is that the reason you were asking about them, you wanted clarification about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe so, Your Honours. This refers also to other things, so they verbatim asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that it refers to other things, but I'm just picking up one of the things that I'm interested in. I want to know from you, are you trying to seek clarification also about the war crimes? And if so, did you get the clarification, finally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I requested intelligence about all the things that they stated in their report. I do not recall their reply, unless you show me a document that could jog my memory and allow me to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That answers my question. Thank you very much. Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 637.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have one final document to show, Exhibit 394, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that book or, sorry, that page, Mr. Husic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, during preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 9 in the B/C/S version and page 13 in the English version. I'm interested in entry number 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you have here in front of you, in B/C/S, the page already. Could you look at the last column, please, starting with --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any signatures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get page 13 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry, in B/C/S the right page was displayed, but it disappeared. It was page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the fifth column -- actually, the English is not -- yes, now it's correct. If you look at the last column 5, whose signatures are these?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: The signatures are mine, starting with item 56, to 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to focus on entry number 59. It says: "Pass on the information that the El Mujahedin Detachment is heading towards Djurica Vis ..." And then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. What am I supposed to do? Should I read it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you comment upon it, since this is obviously an entry made by you, since you signed it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: This is an integral part of a logbook being maintained. Obviously, I entered those entries containing information which, as such, and it's stated here clearly. If you need explanations, I can provide one, but in my opinion, this is very clear. So I wrote this in my capacity as somebody who maintained this log during that specified time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It says next to it: "3rd Corps" --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask the witness: Who is passing on the information and to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the beginning, what is exactly stated under column 4, because we have just a numeral 4. Can we go to the explanation of the column?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To assist the witness, I believe it is page 2 or 3 of this logbook in B/C/S he wants to look at. It's page 2, actually, where there is a kind of headline for column 4. Yes. And in English, it is also page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's stated here "Sender/Recipient" which means the upper reference would be the source or author of information, or whoever relayed the information, and the lower reference is the recipient, to whom it was passed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And can we go back then to entry 59. Let's see who's upper and who's lower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This came from the commander, relayed to the Communications Centre of the El-M Detachment, which means the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How did Mr. -- How did the 3rd Corps commander give this piece of information to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can't really recall. We sat in the same area on the same premises, so if I was keeping this log, I was supposed to be listening to what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said you were --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: It is possible that somebody else relayed that information, but it was said commander ordered that this be so, and this is how I entered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said, "We were at the same location." Which location are you referring to? You said "same premises." I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript says "same area, on the same premises."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I could see, this was maintained at the forward command post, and this is what I refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What's the name of this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can confirm if it's written at the beginning of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You wish to see the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we have the first page shown to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mentioning is made in your entry of Djurica Vis. Do you know what Djurica Vis is?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Djurica Vis is probably a name of an area or of a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you find this location on the map next to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can try to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, please. If the usher could please assist. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have just encircled Djurica Vis. And if I'm not mistaken, the number "6" was given already. Shouldn't it be number "7" now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. You mark a number "7" next to it. Thank you. If I could please tender the map in evidence, and the Prosecution would then have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted in evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 638.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madame Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Could you tell us what this means, what you have written at the end of paragraph 59 of this document? "Be very careful, please." What do you mean by that? Could we see again the English version and the B/C/S version of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the cover page is still displayed at my screen. Could you please go to the page where we can read that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the second page, if I remember, or the third page. "But be careful", be prudent. [In English] "Be careful."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Relay or pass on the information that the El Mujahedin Detachment is to be heading towards Djurica Vis, where there is no one, according to the information provided by the 2nd Corps, but be careful." Which would mean -- and these are not my words, I just relayed that. And that would mean that there are still no accurate information or verified information whether there is somebody there or not, but that the 2nd Corps claims that there is no one there. And this is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, who is to be careful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The El Mujahid Detachment should be careful. This is the recipient, and these are the people who are to carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess this is a convenient time to take the break. We'll come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that. It was for reasons beyond our control. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Husic. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and today I will be examining you on behalf of the Defence of General Rasim Delic. You can answer with a simple "yes" or "no" to most of my questions, since that is the nature of cross-examination. However, if you believe it to be important to add something or clarify, feel free to do so. The only thing I'd like to ask you is to allow a pause between my question and your answers so that the interpreters could finish with interpreting my questions. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you graduated from the Military Academy for Land Forces in Belgrade in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you told us that you completed a specialised course from the intelligence domain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a school.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I see, a school. Thank you. You completed that school just before the war; one could say so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war or, rather, before you began working in the field of intelligence, you had no previous working experience on such jobs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No, until then I had not worked in the field of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you began working in that field, you made use of the knowledge you had from the education you gained before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, I would be correct in saying that your co-workers within the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps lacked such knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For example, Mr. Sejfulah Mrkaljevic, what was his profession?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what his profession was. I do know, however, that before the war he worked in a mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The officers of subordinate commands, and I mean the division and brigade commands, also lacked specialised knowledge in the field of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about Mr. Hajderhodzic, who was the intelligence officer of the 35th Division. He had no military knowledge, did he?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether he had any military knowledge. As regards intelligence, as far as I know, he had no education in that field. I know that before the war, he worked in Krivaja, in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Intelligence Department comprised between 10 and 12 people during 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that is correct for that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Out of those people, and this figure of 10 to 12 people, Mr. Husic, I found it in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, and that is why I'm using it, do you recall that that is what you told the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but also I wasn't sure at the time. It is far too precise for me to be able to say how many people were at any given time, but I presume that the number was such.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of the 10 or 12, you were the only one who had completed the Military Academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The rest of the members of your department had no military knowledge whatsoever; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: It is not. Some did. One of them was about to complete the Military Academy. He was in his final year. And another had completed the Military High School. In any case, there were but a few of them who had any previous military education or background. Most of them did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. However, they had no specialist training from the field of intelligence and reconnaissance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I talked to those people, and they told me that no one had any previous experience before the war from that field.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff and the Command of the 3rd Corps tried to organise -- set up certain courses for training. However, that proved to be insufficient; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: We did what we could. One cannot become an expert overnight. In any case, I believe it was insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that this lack of knowledge and experience had a significant impact on the quality of work of the department? I have in mind the lack of knowledge in the field of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did what our abilities allowed us to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That lack of experience had impact on the use of how to deal with sources and the overall process of handling intelligence data?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The very Department for Intelligence, during 1994 and 1995, worked with difficulty not only because you were short of professionals, but also you were short of equipment and means needed for that type of work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Intelligence Department included both the intelligence and reconnaissance field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, although one cannot really separate the two the way you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Gathering intelligence data depended on the type of reconnaissance or surveillance of enemy positions and units?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Reconnoitering is one of the basic ways of gathering intelligence information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Gathering intelligence data also included the use of data gained through interrogation -- interrogating POWs?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, POWs are certainly a very important source of intelligence information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they are an important source of intelligence information. Would you agree that this important source of information, if one has access to it, is always registered? I mean to say that if there was an interview with a POW and some information was gained, that is put into writing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In all reports, such information was supposed to be included. There was a template, and one of them had to deal with the sources of information. Otherwise, such information would be considered incomplete. If such information came from POWs, one had to stress that it was based on a statement of this and that POW.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Such information gained by interrogating POWs was forwarded for perusal to the organs of your own command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Within the chain that we were a part of, we were obliged to report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then what would follow would be the superior command?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then the adjacent units?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not always, in case it had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you would send such information to adjacent units if it was of importance for their assessment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: We would send information to adjacent units irrespective of the type of source, if we thought that such information had to do with them or that it may assist them, in order to get a fuller picture of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the data stemming from POWs, if verified, was an important source, was important information, in order to assess the situation with the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking. It needn't be so, per se, because maybe they wouldn't be able to hand over any information of that nature that would be of importance. It all depends on the type of POW. There is a great difference between a soldier and an officer, and it also depends on the service they came from or the jobs they held.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you is this: It was always the important information that was recorded?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Such information was taken -- or would be taken into consideration when planning combat activities; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in any case it depended on the decision of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am right in thinking that the processing of POWs was something that superior commands paid special attention to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps put it more plainly?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Superior commands, meaning the General Staff and the Corps Command, demanded the cooperation of military intelligence services and intelligence organs when collating and gathering information gained through POWs; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, at this moment I am putting general questions to you about the issue of POWs. However, I will be more specific when I revert to certain documents. I would like to show Exhibit 626 to the witness at this moment, please. Please have a look at the document. Can you see that this document that came from the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and is dated the 31st of August, 1995, referred to the processing of prisoners of war? It instructs, and it seems that it was sent to the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and the 5th Corps. Please have a look at item 1. You were familiar, within the Corps and generally within the units, that when processing prisoners of war, one had to abide by the provisions of the international laws of war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had to abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, was such instruction forwarded to the lower-ranking units?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can put this document away, since it has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document will be put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at the document shown to you today by the Prosecutor; it is Exhibit 630. Mr. Husic, the Prosecutor showed you this document today, and you said that this was probably a proposal. I would just like to clarify that further. Do you agree with me that this would be a combat document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: This should be an attachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, an attachment to an order for combat operation.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, and so it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the left-hand corner, there should be a signature, that of General Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I said already that this was probably a proposal, a working version, because there is no signature and no time period, and perhaps some other elements are lacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is a name on the last page. Could we please see the last page of the document in both versions. It says here: "Assistant, Captain First Class Edin Husic." Not only that this document was not approved by General Mahmuljin, but even you did not sign this proposal?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is, therefore, simply a working version which never became an official document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Since it was not signed, it is not a valid document. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, under item 2, the Prosecutor indicated -- please take a look at item 2, and this would be the previous page of the English version. I'm sorry for not noticing that the pages do not match. So the previous page in the English version, may it be shown, please. I would like to point your attention to item 2. Here it says: "The focus of intelligence support should be made along the axis ..." et cetera. First of all, I would like you to explain to the Bench what "focus of intelligence support" means. What does this stand for?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: "Focus of intelligence support" means the axis along which one should deploy our forces, in terms of making that area the most interesting one in intelligence terms. So this indicates - and it should be made evident from this attachment - that our forces should be focused along that axis. So special attention should be paid to that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now, given that this is a working version of this document, do you agree that this axis, Svinjasnica-Paljenik-Stog-Miljevici-Vozuca, did not have to be included in the document that was ultimately adopted as an official document, that this could have been altered in different ways?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes. Given that this is a working draft, any part of the document may be subject to changes, to alterations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree that the working version of this document should not be the basis for us establishing that this was really the focus of intelligence support of the 3rd Corps along that axis and during that action?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can really confirm such a thing only if a document approved, signed, was shown to me. And on the basis of such a document, I could verify the actual axis. And since this is a working document, this doesn't really need to be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, may we put this document away, and now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 564.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, first of all, please take a look at this document. It could be said that this was a document by the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps, dated 11th of September, 1995, as a warning delivered to unit commands, to their intelligence organs. Could we scroll the document down so that the witness can see the portion of it bearing the signature. Mr. Husic, could you please take a look at this document and tell me whether you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can verify that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please, if we can zoom out so that we see the whole document, so that we can elicit an explanation to what this note "All Commands" means. That means to all subordinate units' commands or to commands specified here?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: It says to unit commands, and then in the lower portion it is indicated which unit commands should have this document delivered to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. It can be seen that it was delivered to the 35th Division. Do you agree that you delivered this warning to the intelligence organ of the 35th Division to the effect that they are obliged to consolidate those reports to all their units, including the El Mujahedin Detachment and the 2nd Manoeuvre Battalion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says so, that they are to consolidate in their report the reports of all units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, I would like to ask you this: At the beginning of the document, it is said that some units failed to provide intelligence, and in the last sentence of the document it is insisted that information, including the El Mujahedin Detachment, should be delivered. Please, it is correct, is it not, that you did not receive reports until the date specified here and that this was the reason -- I mean the 11th September, and that this was the reason for you insisting that the 35th Division consolidate and include in their report the reports from the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: As can be seen from this document, the 35th Division did deliver their report. This can be gleaned from the first sentence. However, at the end of the sentence, we warn the 35th Division they should consolidate reports from other units, which probably means that in their previously-submitted report, they failed to include the reports from the other two units which were at the time subordinate to them, and they were under their command and control. And this is why this warning was sent. Apparently they had not delivered. Had they delivered, this warning would not have been sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we put this document away, please. I would like the witness to be shown document D552, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, for the record may I state that this is a document of the 3rd Corps Command --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- dated 13 of September, 1995. Can this document be scrolled down so that we can see the signature. Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of the then-commander, Brigadier Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you can see from the title, this document deals with the treatment of captured documentation and war prisoners. I would like to attraction your attention to item 3 of this document. And since you worked on intelligence, this paragraph makes reference to such work. This section stipulates that interrogation of war prisoners should be conducted by senior officers from intelligence bodies as a priority and then by the military security bodies. Do you agree that this practice has been ordered by the 3rd Corps Command to the subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this order, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, and since you worked in 3rd Corps, you had occasion to apply commanders' orders in this respect. I would like to ask you whether this was something that was required and had to be abided by on the part of the lower commands.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this was the reason why we sent this order. But may I provide a comment pertaining to item 3? For us, it was important that first intelligence officers conduct the interviews because data may become obsolete and unusable or partly unusable, and this is why we wanted to achieve, through this order, to give priority to intelligence organs. And for security, military security organs to take over afterwards. This was the purpose of this paragraph within this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, may this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 639.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we show Exhibit 629 to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You may recall this is a document shown to you by the Prosecutor, and in connection with this you said -- as far as I can recall, you said that you signed this document. This is a document of the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command, dated 27th of May, 1995, and concerns information on enemy. I would like to ask you this: Please explain this to us. This is reflective of the practice of you delivering to the adjacent units some information for their use, and in this case, this is the 2nd Corps; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, we had our number here, so this was a usual practice. It was not important just to hold on to some information. It was very important to send information and intelligence to others so that they can use them to the extent they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, the Prosecutor asked you something about a portion of this document, and now I'm going to ask you about the portion of the document under item 2, saying that unofficial information claims that the El-M Detachment captured aggressor soldiers and a tank. What I'm interested in is, for you to tell me is: What was the practice and what was the treatment of unofficial information, what "unofficial information" meant to you and to adjacent units?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: "Unofficial information" was unverified information, unvalidated. By its very nature, it is unofficial. Whoever wrote this may have obtained such information from a source presumed not to be capable of being in possession of such information, and this is why it was stated in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So when it is stated in such documents that information is unverified or unofficial, this means that such information is not verified and is not credible; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document has already been tendered, and can we have it put away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You asked what I think is a very important question, but I don't remember. It got clouded with other things that you said later, so it was not answered. Your question was: "What was the practice and what was the treatment of unofficial information?" I would like to hear an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, did you understand what His Honour asked you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I've understood. Your Honours, all unverified, unofficial information had to be subject to scrutiny, which doesn't mean that one was always successful in verification. It happened that an information came from a single source and it was verified as coming from a single source, which does not mean if information is available, that you can verify it in all cases. But as such, it holds a meaning or a significance, or information can be important even if you know that something is not going on. So if somebody fails to provide a report, it means that they failed in their duty, but if they report that there's nothing to report, then we know what -- where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I just want to follow up my question. My question then is: Was this particular information scrutinised and verified? And if so, what was the result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In respect of this specific piece of information, I cannot recall whether it was or was not verified, scrutinised. Usual practice would dictate that in the subsequent report, the unit were supposed to confirm or reject such information, or maybe we would seek additional clarification or verification. But on the basis of this document, this cannot be determined, and my memory does not allow me to give you a specific or precise answer to this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up on this, Mr. Husic, on this question by His Honour. Mr. Husic, it's correct, is it not, that the duty of a subordinated unit that forwards an unofficial, unverified information, to verify it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They are supposed to follow up on it, but you cannot seek that they do so in all cases. If they report such information, then it was only logical for them to continue, because this was their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, I'd like to ask you as follows: If they were to obtain verified information, that they would be duty-bound to forward it to the Corps Command; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have this document put away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may be put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like the witness to see Exhibit 554. Could we zoom in on the first part of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, this is a document of the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command, dated the 24th of July, 1995. It's a report sent to the forward command post of the 3rd Corps at Orahovo, to Edin Husic. This is you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down, please, so as to be able to see the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is signed by Captain Mrkaljevic, Sejfulah. Let us go back to the top, please, in both versions for Their Honours to be able to see. I wanted to ask you this, Mr. Husic: This was the 24th July 1995. It seems that you were at the forward command post at Orahovo. Do you remember whether, on this day, the 24th of July, 1995, you were at Orahovo, and what is Orahovo, first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: It states here the forward command post of the 3rd Corps; Orahovo is the location. Whether at that very time I was there, I truly cannot say. However, this document states that I sent it from that place, and I'd say this confirms your thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the document say you sent it or does the document say it is sent to you? I see it's to Edin Husic, personally, and I thought it comes from somebody other than yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Your Honour. It states that this report was sent to me, personally. The abbreviation and slash "N/R" would actually mean "Attention." "Edin Husic," that would be me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, probably there was a misinterpretation. If I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you said, Witness, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going by what I saw in the English translation. It said: "However, this document states that I sent it from that place, and I would say this confirms your thesis." That's line 8 to 9, page 78.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We've clarified that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that this document arrived by telegraph on the 24th of July, 1995, at 1946? This is when the document was processed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down, please. Please have a look at the part of the document beginning with: "Contact." Could we please scroll down or, rather, go to page 3 of the English. That is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you read the part beginning: "Contact from a superior from the El Mujahedin Detachment with the aim to take possession of certain documentation ..." and to the end?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: The entire passage?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but to yourself.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this document justifies that the commander of the 3rd Corps approved that contact should be made with the El Mujahedin Detachment, and that was asked of Captain Mrkaljevic, in order to try and establish contact with prisoners at the camp of the El Mujahedin Detachment? Does it say so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that calls for me reading the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this telegram, do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the contents of the telegram, and I mean the access to POWs on the 24th of July, 1995, as regards that, did you have any conversation with Mr. Sejfulah Mrkaljevic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I truly cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot remember. Your Honours, I would like to invoke the testimony of the 10th of October, 2007, page 3892 [Realtime transcript read in error "8392"], lines 18 to 21. I will quote: "Mr. Mrkaljevic, if someone were to say the following ..." I'd like you to listen to what I'm about to read and I would like to ask you for your comment. Would it be true and correct: "In conversation with Mr. Edin Husic, he suggested I should not raise the issue of captured soldiers of the 1st Prnjavor Brigade, since another service was working on the issue, meaning that I did not report to the commander on the issue of prisoners." Is it correct that you suggested to the author of this document here -- or rather do you remember whether you ever suggested anything of that nature to anyone?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that. Why would I suggest to someone not to do something if he had already been tasked with something? That is one thing. Another thing, formally speaking, I had no right to interfere with the commander's decision. In this specific case, irrespective of what I can remember or not, he personally was tasked with that. Neither was it my practice, nor do I do that today or ever, to interfere or change a commander's decision. The person tasked with something is obliged to see that through the way he was tasked. I never did such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, even had you wanted to, you wouldn't have been able to change the commander's decision?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had no right to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, just so that we don't get lost later when we want to check your reference, the transcript says "page 8392". It should be "3892".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "38".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript said "83", so I just want to make sure that when later we read this, we go to the correct page to get the information. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The 10th of October, 2007, page 3892, lines 18 through 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this, another question, Mr. Mrkaljevic -- sorry, Mr. Husic. How far is Orahovo from this area of Zavidovici? How far is it from Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Orahovo and the area of Sarajevo, from Zavidovici, I'd say about 200 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what in Sarajevo now, Mr. Husic? Is it the distance between Orahovo and Zavidovici or is it the distance between Sarajevo and Zavidovici? I'm sorry to do this to you, Madam Vidovic, but we've got to get clarity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Orahovo is far closer to Sarajevo than to another location. I don't know whether the distance was exactly 200 kilometres. It was my approximation, having in mind that from Sarajevo to Zavidovici, it is around 200 kilometres, if that may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not of assistance. The question put to you was: "How far is Orahovo from Zavidovici?" Just don't mention Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For sure, it's over 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that help, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about certain events in September 1995. We saw some documents, I showed some of them to you, which demanded the gathering of information about POWs and their transfer to the 3rd Corps. You confirmed that such information was registered and forwarded for further use; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Provided that the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps received information on a large number of POWs, say 50, the department would register that and would demand access to those prisoners, would it not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can show Exhibit 636 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Mrkaljevic -- sorry, Mr. Husic, I'd like to ask you this: Did you, in September 1995, ever -- and when I say "you," I don't mean you, personally, but the department -- did you in any way receive any information on 50 POWs? Can you recall any such thing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I truly cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have this document before us. It was shown to you today by the Prosecutor. Please focus on it. It is a document sent by the 3rd Corps Command, its Intelligence Department, dated the 12th of September, 1995. Let us scroll down to the bottom to see the signature block. Do you remember this document, Mr. Husic? You were able to recall that it was you who signed it.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will also recall that you were questioned by the Prosecutor about the contents, and I have a question relating to that. On the 12th of September, you wrote: "Currently, we have four POWs being processed." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, so it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have the English scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 2, Your Honour, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, had you had information on that day, that there were more prisoners of war, you would have mentioned a number, would you not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I believe so. We would put in the data we had. That would be reflected in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put to you one part of it which had to do with groups of Chetniks numbered between 40 to 60 from the 14th Light Brigade. You remember, I hope, that were supposed to be in the area of Kablovac, Prokop, and Stoska Kamenica. You were marking those on the map and numbering them. Do you remember that? There is also another part -- another group, I believe, mentioned here. I believe they were called "Cigini Panteri". I'd like to ask you the following. It says here Cigini Panteri are in the following locations: They used the wooded part towards Stosnica village, trying to pull out towards Kablovac. Mr. Husic, did you ever at any moment until the end of the war find out that any of these people or any of the groups or, rather, 40 to 60 soldiers from the 14th Brigade, or the Cigini Panteri, that a group of such people was captured; did you ever find out such a thing during the war while you were working on these tasks?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I truly do not remember such a thing. The information contained therein states the same thing you told me. This is what the POWs stated. Whether that was correct or not, we did not know; we merely forwarded information to the users. I cannot recall that we received any information on such a large number of soldiers, concerning their fate or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You agree such an information may indicate that they met with different fates, that they had succeeded in pulling out of this encirclement; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course, it can mean that, but as you can see in this report, we clearly stated that the probable intentions were to use this wooded area, but also it confirms that the information that we obtained from this source allows us to make estimates but not to be sure or certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, it was possible that those groups of people got killed fighting members of units of the 2nd or 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or anybody else; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course. It was equally possible that they withdraw or as possible as the possibility that this information is not true. Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if you had received a report on the capturing of a group of 40 to 60 soldiers, would you have demanded an interview to be conducted with those people so that you could obtain intelligence? Let me ask you this again.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course, this is regulated in the order, and this is why that order that we saw was sent during that period. I believe the document we saw a couple of minutes ago, for us this was an important source of data, irrespective of the validity or invalidity of such data. What was important is to have data.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we put this document away, Your Honours, and I think that I will have enough time to show just one document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document will be put away. I guess it's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honours. May we show D554 to the witness, please. It seems that this is also a 3rd Corps Command's document, its Intelligence Department. The date is the 14th -- the 16th of September, 1995, entitled "Notification about the enemy," addressed to the Command of the 37th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the signature block. Could we scroll down to it, please. Are you able to recognise this signature, Mr. Husic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems to state "MS/A." Could this indicate the author?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: It should be "MS/E" which would be "Sejfulah Mrkaljevic."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can we scroll up to the top of the document. And Sejfulah Mrkaljevic is your associate, a member of your staff in the Intelligence Department? Is that the person we discussed a couple of minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: You probably did not speak to all prisoners of war, and you did not perform all the tasks in your Intelligence Department, but nevertheless I'd like to ask you this: There is information about one of the prisoners of war, Banovic, Novica, there are some vital statistics of his, and the next sentence says: "When captured, he was in possession of an automatic rifle and he was wounded on the left upper arm." I would like to ask you about a principle. Please, do you agree that documents recorded the situation and the status of that prisoner of war, that he was captured, wounded; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: This document shows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was important to describe that status?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I agree, was this may influence his statement to us, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean it can influence the accuracy of the data he was about to provide; is that what you meant? Could you expound on that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. If he's wounded, he may be in the state of shock, which means that he'd be able to provide a partial statement or the statement provided under shock, in a state of shock, could be -- could prompt us to doubt the data provided by him. I believe that this would be important from that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get clarification before we go. The very first sentence of this document, sir, says: "In the initial questioning of soldiers of the so-called RS Army ..." I'm not sure. Can you tell us whether we also have the status of the rest of the soldiers that were captured, because this seems to be talking about the status of one soldier only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's stated here, "in the initial questioning" or the first questioning, this could mean that those persons were going to be interrogated again. And what is contained there is what we obtained as data during the first or initial questioning, and this is supposed to mean that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but if this document is giving us the status of Banovic, Novica, shouldn't it give us the status of all the soldiers that have been captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I may agree with you about this. If no status is described, as pertains the others, then it may have been left out. Maybe this was emphasised because it was important for his status. I don't know what the condition of the others was. I would have to read the entire document to be able to provide a precise answer to the question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I thought you said, and I may be wrong here, I thought you said that it would be practice to tabulate the status of prisoners of war because that is important to the reliability of the information you extract from them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this, I can only partly agree with you. We did not record their condition or status. What was important to us was information from them, because they were not within the area of our competence. But as far as our practice was, one should read the entire document so that we can obtain this piece of information. I cannot claim, nor can I recall, that in the Intelligence Department we maintained records on the condition of people, whether they were wounded or not, and in this respect I really cannot confirm. And this is the only explanation I can give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But then if, then, this document doesn't tell us anything about the status of the other soldiers, what then can -- what conclusion can we draw in terms of the practice that you referred to, the practice of recording the status of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably you have not understood me well. I did not say that we had a practice of maintaining records of the condition of such people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise. If you didn't say so, I apologise. Thank you so much. Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, aside from the Intelligence Section or Department, there was also the Security Department that was in charge of the witnesses; right? Or, rather, of the POWs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible that the Information Department was registering data such as these data concerning, let's say, prisoner Banovic, Novica, only because they had gotten information from that prisoner and that the information was not registered according to which your department did not have information regarding those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that presumption is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one minute so I can be finished with this document. Let us clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned several witnesses [as interpreted] -- or this document mentions several witnesses [as interpreted]. Do you agree that you recently saw a document referring to four other prisoners of war; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, but really we cannot make the distinction between the first and the other, because in the previous document that we saw, we -- that document does not contain the names and surnames of the prisoners of war. This one does. Therefore, I cannot confirm whether this -- these two documents refer to the same people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's understandable. But this report to the 37th Division makes mention of the data provided by this Novica Banovic. The other people referred to in this document are not prisoners of war. They are people he provides information about. Could you go through this document and clarify this or confirm this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: In that case, I would like you to give me some time to go through this document. And another thing. The copy that I'm being shown in Bosnian is not very legible, at least at the level of resolution shown here. If you could give me some time to read the entire document, I will be in a position to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can revisit this document at any rate, should we do it now or later, given that I'm not finished with my cross-examination. I'm sure to be re-examining this document, because I've not finished dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would suggest we deal with it at the next session. And do remember, Madam Vidovic, based on what you said just now to the witness, that my questions were based on the very first sentence in the document, and not the people that are being talked about in the document. Do you suggest that this is a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, we are not done with you. We will ask you to come back on Thursday, the 25th of October, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II, not this courtroom, Courtroom II. This is because tomorrow is a United Nations holiday. We are not working. For now, you are excused. You may stand down until the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may stand down, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner. You wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It has disappeared in the meantime from the transcript. I believe it was on page 91, lines 19 and 20, the witness has given an answer [sic], and it was twice referred to "witnesses." I don't speak B/C/S, so I didn't understand what the witness was saying in original, but maybe the transcript or the audio can be revisited. Probably the witness meant to say "prisoners of war," but it was twice noted "witnesses."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 91?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 90, lines 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my learned colleague Neuner. It's obviously a reference to prisoners of war, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I assumed so, too, but I didn't understand the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it says: "That document does not contain the names and surnames of the prisoners of war." That's what it says: "This one does. Therefore, I cannot confirm whether these documents refer to the same people." Is that what you're referring to, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My problem is at this late stage, I cannot stop the transcript here. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, there is a transcript you can control if you have two screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend Neuner is trying to point your attention to page 90, lines 16 and 17, and 16 -- and it says: "You mentioned several prisoners ... " And what is reflected in the transcript is "witnesses."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what you are saying, that those "witnesses" should be replaced with "prisoners of war"? Okay. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Thank you, Mr. Neuner. The Court stands adjourned to Thursday, the 25th of October, at 9.00 in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.12 p.m.,
